blockers.message: the review record has no `## code.review` section, while roles were active at it
R-skeptic-1 (The merge key rests on an assumption the design's own context contradicts) is high and still open; fix it, or a human accepts the risk or defers it
R-skeptic-2 (Deleting the merged records is irreversible, with no way back) is high and still open; fix it, or a human accepts the risk or defers it

findings.evidence:
Since an e-mail address identifies exactly one person, the job groups
customers by lower-cased e-mail, keeps the oldest record of each group,
moves the others' orders to it and deletes the others.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Customers are merged by e-mail
findings.recommendation: The Context of the same design states "Business customers often share a purchasing mailbox (`orders@acme.example`) between several buyers, each with their own customer record and billing address." With e-mail as the sole key, the job would fold distinct buyers into one record, attach their orders to another buyer and delete their names and billing addresses. Either restrict the merge to records that are verifiably the same person (e-mail plus name and/or billing address, or guest records only), or state and verify why shared mailboxes cannot occur. Add a spec scenario "Two buyers share a mailbox" with the expected outcome, and a task and test for it.
findings.title: The merge key rests on an assumption the design's own context contradicts

findings.evidence: moves the others' orders to it and deletes the others.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: Customers are merged by e-mail
findings.recommendation: The job hard-deletes customer rows nightly and the plan gives no backup, merge log, soft delete, dry run or staged rollout; a wrong merge (see R-skeptic-1) cannot be undone, since the original customer_id of each moved order is lost. Record each merge (kept id, deleted id, its fields, moved order ids) or soft-delete, and plan a dry-run first run, with a task that verifies an unmerge is possible.
findings.title: Deleting the merged records is irreversible, with no way back

findings.evidence: A nightly job SHALL merge customer records that share an e-mail address into the oldest one, moving their orders to it.
findings.recommendation: The scenarios are only "Two records, one e-mail" and "No duplicate". The requirement does not say whether e-mails differing in case are the same (the design says "lower-cased e-mail", the spec says "share an e-mail address"), nor what happens to the name and billing address of the deleted records when they differ from the kept one, nor what happens with three or more records or two with the same created_at. Add scenarios for case differences, conflicting fields and ties, so the requirement can be checked.
findings.title: The spec covers only the happy path and leaves conflicting fields undefined

findings.recommendation: The proposal adds "A nightly job merges customers that share an e-mail address." — a scheduled job that someone must deploy, run and monitor — and the job rewrites orders.customer_id and deletes customer rows in existing data. Tick operations and migration, or give on each line the reason they do not apply, so their experts review the scheduling, the failure handling and the transformation of existing data.
findings.title: The plan schedules and runs a data-deleting job with operations and migration unticked

findings.evidence: Guest checkouts create a new customer each time; support sees five records for one person.
findings.recommendation: The cause named in the Why is app/checkout.py `guest_checkout`, which always runs "INSERT INTO customers" per order. The plan leaves it as is, so duplicates reappear every day until the next run. Consider whether reusing the existing guest record at checkout (with the same identity rule as R-skeptic-1) would solve the Why with less risk, the nightly job then only cleaning historical data.
findings.title: The plan cleans up duplicates without stopping their source
